idiom_name: callback signature + registration + stored callback with context + dispatcher invocation
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define the callback signature (completion, failure and optionally progress), pass or register the callback together with its per-operation context, retain both until the work finishes, and dispatch the result or error according to an explicit contract. State the contract tuple—timing (inline or deferred), cardinality (once or repeated), execution context, ownership/cancellation and error delivery—because the initiating frame is gone when a deferred callback runs. The service sees only the signature, never the client type. The two forms—synchronous (during the call, e.g. comparators) and deferred (after the call returns, e.g. I/O completions)—must not be mixed accidentally.
pitfalls: Invoking the callback inline instead of through the dispatcher leaks a synchronous path into an asynchronous contract, so callers see two different orders.
Completing more than once (both the success and the failure path, or a retry that re-invokes) breaks the single-completion assumption every caller relies on.
Letting the callback reach back into the service's own state without a defined reentrancy rule invites deadlocks and lost updates.
Capturing the dispatcher's thread in a blocking call: the callback becomes responsible for event loop throughput.
Forgetting to null out the stored callback after completion, causing the context and any objects it references to be retained for the lifetime of the service.
Treating a repeated event listener as a one-shot completion: the second event is dropped or mutates freed state; instead use a repeated-subscription contract with explicit unregister.
Assuming the callback runs on the initiating thread: UI updates or thread-confined state fail when the dispatcher differs; instead state the executor and hop to the required thread.

Bridging an error-first callback without guarding resolve or reject: a late or duplicate callback settles a promise twice or loses the error; instead detach the callback and settle one branch exactly once.

Wrong move: assuming the provider stops calling once your work finishes -> libcurl documents that socket and timer callbacks fire at any time, even after all transfers complete or during curl_multi_cleanup, so a client torn down early receives callbacks into freed context -> instead keep the context and handlers registered until the library itself signals final teardown.

Wrong move: handling only the success tag of a tagged completion -> gRPC's CompletionQueue delivers an event for every initiated operation with ok=false when the call fails or the server shuts down, so success-only handlers leak the in-flight context and miss the shutdown path -> instead treat every tagged completion as a state transition and branch on the ok flag.

Wrong move: signalling async failure by throwing from or through the callback -> the exception escapes the initiating stack (dispatcher or C ABI) and cannot reach the original caller, so it is lost or terminates the process -> instead carry failure inside the callback signature as a Result, status or error-first argument, as Swift's Result-based completion handlers and Node's error-first convention do.
